description: I'm passionate about AI, satellite imagery, Earth observation and scientific innovation. I'm building DELTA SENTINEL AI for NASA Space Apps 2026, combining AI and SAR data to address real-world challenges. I'm looking for motivated teammates skilled in Python, machine learning, GIS, remote sensing, SAR processing and web development. Creativity, teamwork and curiosity are welcome!
summary:
DELTA SENTINEL AI is a web platform that turns satellite radar data into clear maps of water change on the Wouri estuary in Douala, Cameroon.

What we developed: a web app (FastAPI, React, MapLibre) fed by a processing pipeline. Using NASA open data (NISAR L-band radar, OPERA DSWx-S1 water maps, GPM rainfall and SRTM terrain), we build a water mask for each date. A user picks a source and two dates, and the platform classifies water gain, water loss and stable water, measures each area in km² on a metric grid, and displays everything on an interactive map with a before/after swipe. Results export as GeoJSON, CSV or a printable report.

How it addresses the challenge:  radar sees day and night, through clouds, so it can monitor places where optical satellites are often blind. We make this hard-to-read data understandable for non-specialists, and we show source, dates, method and limits with every result.

Why it matters:  floods and wetland change affect communities and mangrove ecosystems in tropical deltas. Transparent, traceable radar monitoring helps researchers and local organizations understand how surfaces change. We present observed change, not forecasts, and claim no validated accuracy yet.
details:
DELTA SENTINEL AI turns satellite radar data into clear maps of water change around Douala and the Wouri estuary in Cameroon. The idea is simple: the user picks two dates and presses one button, and the platform shows where water appeared, disappeared or stayed the same. To make this possible, we start from NASA open data, namely NISAR L-band radar, OPERA DSWx-S1 water maps derived from Sentinel-1, GPM IMERG daily rainfall and SRTM terrain. Python scripts first crop each scene to the study area and build a water mask for each date. Then, when two dates from the same source are compared, the backend places both masks on a 30 metre grid, labels each pixel as water gain, water loss or stable water, and measures the areas in square kilometres. Finally, the result appears on an interactive map with a before and after slider, together with charts of water surface and rainfall and a short analysis sheet, and it can be exported as GeoJSON, CSV or a printable report.

Because radar sees through clouds, day and night, the tool works where optical satellites are often blind, and it gives non-specialists a clear picture of surface water change without asking them to handle raw radar files. Moreover, every result shows its source, dates, method and limits, so anyone can check it.

We chose Douala because it is a city of our country that is constantly hit by floods, and because it is a maritime city where the sea, the estuary and the rains meet. Our intended impact is therefore to help researchers, students and local organizations follow how water and wetlands change in tropical deltas, as a first step toward better awareness. However, we want to be clear that this is a tool to monitor observed change: it is not a flood forecast and not an alert system.

To build it, we used Python, FastAPI, GeoPandas, Rasterio, h5py and NumPy for the processing and the API, and JavaScript with React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS and Recharts for the interface. The data comes from NASA Earthdata and the ASF DAAC, and we worked on ordinary laptops without any special hardware. The code and documentation are available on GitHub.

What makes the project creative is that, instead of producing one more static flood map, we built a small comparison studio around a before and after swipe. Likewise, we chose to display uncertainty and limits on screen, so that radar results are understandable and honest rather than impressive and unclear.

Finally, we considered several factors along the way. L-band NISAR and C-band Sentinel-1 do not measure the same thing, so we never mix them. In addition, urban areas and mangroves can confuse radar, rainfall data is only regional, and our NISAR water threshold is not yet calibrated with field data. For these reasons, we have not claimed any accuracy figure, since the results are not yet validated against an independent reference. Our next steps are to add an uncertainty class and to run that validation.

Thank you.
